indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.1.2.1: Recognise materials as important resources for providing human needs
indicator.objective: Know the common properties of materials such as soft, hard, rough, smooth, opaque, transparent, bendable

skills.description: Name the common properties of materials
Identify a material's property by touching or looking at it
Sort materials based on a given property
Link a property of a material to why it is used for a particular product

misconceptions: Soft means weak or easily broken.
Transparent and smooth are the same thing.

questions.stem: What word describes a material that you can see through clearly, like a clean window?
questions.explanation: A transparent material, like clear glass, allows you to see through it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse transparent with just being clean.

questions.stem: How does a piece of cotton wool feel?
hints: You use it for a baby.
questions.explanation: Cotton wool is soft because it is fluffy and easy to squeeze.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think cotton wool is hard because it is packed tightly.

questions.stem: What word describes a material that you CANNOT see through, like a brick wall?
hints: You cannot see what is behind it.
questions.explanation: An opaque material does not let light pass through, so you cannot see through it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think opaque means the material is black or dark.

questions.stem: Which of these materials is rough to touch?
hints: It is used for rubbing wood.
questions.explanation: Sandpaper has a rough surface because it is covered with tiny hard grains.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse rough with just being dirty.

questions.stem: If you can bend a material easily without it breaking, we say it is...
hints: You can change its shape with your hands.
questions.explanation: A bendable material can be bent or twisted into different shapes.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think bendable means it will break easily.

questions.stem: Which group contains only hard materials?
hints: Which group has things that are solid and difficult to squeeze?
questions.explanation: A stone, an iron nail, and wood are all hard materials.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think wood is soft because it floats.

questions.stem: Kofi is sorting materials. He puts a glass cup and a clear plastic bottle in one group. What property are they sharing?
questions.explanation: Both the glass cup and the clear plastic bottle are transparent.
questions.misconception: Pupils may focus on the shape or size instead of the property.

questions.stem: Why is glass a good material for making windows?
options: Because it is transparent and lets in light
questions.explanation: Glass is used for windows because it is transparent, allowing light in and allowing people to see outside.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect the property of transparency to the use of windows.

questions.stem: Ama has two spoons: one made of metal and one made of plastic. Which one is smoother and feels colder to touch?
questions.explanation: The metal spoon is smoother and feels colder to touch than the plastic spoon.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plastic is always colder than metal.

questions.stem: Which property of a material tells you it is soft?
options: You can easily squeeze it and change its shape
It makes a loud sound when you hit it
hints: It changes shape when you press it.
questions.explanation: Soft materials are easy to squeeze and do not keep their shape when pressed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think soft means it is wet.

questions.stem: Why do we use clay for making pots?
options: Because it is bendable and can be moulded
hints: Think about how a pot is made.
Clay can be shaped by hand.
questions.explanation: Clay is used for pots because it is bendable and can be moulded into different shapes before it is baked hard.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not realize clay is bendable before baking.

questions.stem: Name one material that is transparent and one material that is opaque.
answer: transparent: glass, clear plastic, water; opaque: wood, stone, metal, brick
questions.explanation: Glass is transparent, while wood is opaque.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name objects instead of materials.

questions.stem: What do we call a material that you cannot see through?
questions.explanation: A material you cannot see through is opaque.
questions.misconception: Pupils may say 'dark' instead of opaque.

questions.stem: Why do we use rubber to make the wheels of a car (tyres)?
options: Because it is hard and breaks easily
Because it is rough and sticky
Because it is bendable and strong
hints: Tyres need to grip the road.
They must not break on stones.
questions.explanation: Rubber is used for tyres because it is bendable and strong, which helps it absorb shocks and not break easily.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think rubber is used because it is soft and weak.

questions.stem: Ama has a wooden block, a piece of glass, a plastic ruler, and a sheet of paper. Which group has only materials that are opaque?
questions.explanation: Wood and paper are opaque; they do not let light pass through.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think thin paper is transparent.

questions.stem: A tailor wants to make a shirt. Which material is best and why?
options: Cloth, because it is soft and bendable
questions.explanation: Cloth is the best material for a shirt because it is soft and bendable, making it comfortable to wear.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose metal for its strength without considering comfort.

questions.stem: Kofi has a material that is opaque and hard. What could it be?
hints: It does not let light through.
questions.explanation: A metal nail is both opaque and hard.
questions.misconception: Pupils may confuse hard with bendable.

questions.stem: Explain why glass is used to make the windshields of cars.

criteria.description: States that this allows the driver to see clearly outside

hints: The driver needs to see the road.
questions.explanation: Glass is used for car windshields because it is transparent, allowing the driver to see the road clearly.

questions.stem: A farmer needs a material to cover his crops so that sunlight can reach them but rain cannot. Which type of material should he use?
options: A transparent material like clear plastic
questions.explanation: Clear plastic is transparent (lets sunlight in) but also waterproof (keeps rain out), making it ideal for a greenhouse or crop cover.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose wood or metal because they are strong, without considering the need for sunlight.

questions.stem: Why would a metal bucket be a BAD choice for carrying water if it has a hole in it, while a plastic bucket is good?
options: Metal is always weaker than plastic
Metal is harder and cannot be moulded
hints: Can you easily fix a hole in metal without special tools?
Plastic can be melted and moulded.
questions.explanation: A metal bucket with a hole cannot be easily fixed because metal is hard and cannot be moulded by hand, whereas plastic can be moulded or welded more easily. Also, metal might rust. (Note: Focus is on metal being hard and not easily changed).
questions.misconception: Pupils may not know the difference between moulding and hammering.

questions.stem: You need a material to make a raincoat. It must not let water pass through, and it must be bendable so you can move your arms. Which material is best?
questions.explanation: A thick plastic sheet is best because it is waterproof (opaque to water) and bendable, allowing movement.
questions.misconception: Pupils may choose cotton because clothes are usually made of cloth, ignoring the 'waterproof' requirement.
